contradiction.viewer_thinks: 1816's bizarre weather was a local curse — some regions just got unlucky
contradiction.actually: one eruption on the far side of the planet reorganized the weather of the whole Northern Hemisphere

beats.narration: In June 1816, snow fell on New England. Frost struck every summer month. No one could say why.
beats.claim: 1816 brought anomalous summer cold and June snow to New England with no visible cause at the time
beats.visual_question: what could turn summer into winter?
beats.visual_answer: a New England field under June snow, the cause nowhere in sight

beats.narration: The seed was April 1815, on Sumbawa: Mount Tambora exploded — the largest eruption in recorded history — losing a kilometre of summit.
beats.claim: Mount Tambora erupted in April 1815 in the largest eruption in recorded history, losing over a kilometre of summit height
beats.visual_answer: the volcano's blast column with more than a kilometre of the summit blown away

beats.narration: Its real weapon was invisible: tens of millions of tonnes of sulfur into the stratosphere — above the rain — a veil around the planet.
beats.claim: Tambora injected tens of millions of tonnes of sulfur into the stratosphere, where global winds spread a planet-wide veil
beats.visual_question: how does one volcano reach the whole planet?
beats.visual_answer: a sulfur veil circling the globe in the stratosphere, above the weather

beats.narration: The veil scatters sunlight back to space. The world cooled by roughly half a degree. To a ripening crop, that was catastrophe.
beats.claim: stratospheric sulfate aerosols scattered sunlight and cooled the planet by roughly half a degree Celsius in 1816
beats.visual_question: how cold can a veil of droplets make the world?
beats.visual_answer: sunlight scattering off the veil, with global temperature down about half a degree

beats.narration: Then came 1816: June snow on New England, frost month after month, and the growing season collapsed.
beats.claim: in 1816 June snow fell on New England and killing frosts recurred through the summer months
beats.visual_question: what does a failed summer look like?
beats.visual_answer: June snow on a New England field, frost lines through young crops

beats.narration: Harvests failed on three continents. Food riots spread — historians still call it the last great subsistence crisis of the Western world.
beats.claim: the 1816 harvest failures brought soaring prices, famine and food riots; historians describe it as the last great subsistence crisis of the Western world
beats.visual_question: what does half a degree do to dinner?
beats.visual_answer: empty granary sacks and bread queues: the harvest that never came

beats.narration: For years, no one connected the skies to the mountain. The veil settled — one mountain, one planet, one atmosphere.
beats.claim: the 1816 climate anomaly was traced to the 1815 Tambora eruption only decades later, after the veil had settled
beats.visual_question: so what was the Year Without a Summer?
beats.visual_answer: a planet-scale echo of one eruption, and the first lesson that the atmosphere is one connected system
